One dewback, a yoke, and a light two-wheeled platform to stand on. It is the fastest thing a scavenger clan can build out of scrap, and it is fast only where the ground is already flat and packed.

Dewbacks are big grey-green lizards that do not hurry and do not need to. They drink at dawn, walk through the worst of the heat without complaint, and will keep a steady pace long after a warm-blooded animal has lain down in whatever shade it can find.

Off a road the chariot is close to useless — the wheels are narrow, they cut into soft sand, and the rider spends more time hauling it free than riding it.

A pair of dewbacks in double harness and a shooting platform braced over the axle. One hand drives; the other stands behind the rail and works whatever the clan could hang off it.

The dewbacks are the reason it works. They are slow to start and impossible to stop, they do not spook at noise the way a ronto does, and they will walk straight at something that is shooting back — which is a rarer quality in a draft animal than it sounds.

It is not cavalry. It is a way to put a shooter somewhere they could not have walked to, and to get them out again afterwards.

Two rontos in front of a four-wheeled wagon with a hide roof stretched over hoops. The roof is not comfort. It is the difference between arriving and arriving with heatstroke.

Rontos are enormous, dun-coloured and profoundly nervous. They will carry a house across open pan all day and then bolt at a shadow, so the harness is built to come apart faster than it goes on, and nobody sensible sleeps under the wheels.

Leather strapping under the bed takes the worst of the ruts out. Three can ride in the back without arriving bruised, which on a two-day crossing is worth more than speed.

Two banthas and a two-wheeled cart. Nothing on this world moves more weight for less trouble, and nothing looks less impressive doing it.

A bantha is a mountain of shaggy hide under a pair of spiral horns, and it is stupid in the specific way that makes an animal useful — it will lean into a load until the load moves or the harness breaks, and it does not form an opinion about which. They eat anything with roots, they carry their own water for days, and the Tuskens have built an entire way of living on them for good reason.

Use it for salvage: hull plate, machinery, whatever came out of a wreck too heavy to carry. It is slow, it is terrible off a road, and it will still be doing this long after the fast things have shaken themselves apart.

Two eopies in harness, and a flatbed of lashed scrap riding on runners because wheels drown in soft sand.

They are patient, sour-smelling animals with long necks and a hide like cracked leather, and they will walk all day on almost nothing. Water they need. Food they mostly find, chewing whatever grey thing is rooted between the rocks. They complain constantly through their snouts, they spit when handled badly, and they are worth every bit of it — an eopie team will cross open pan in the heat of the day and be ready to do it again after a night's rest and a trough.

The sled is the point. Runners spread the load where a cart would dig in, so you can haul a wreck's worth of salvage back across the flats instead of picking through it for what fits in a pack.
